reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Benign proliferation of male glandular breast tissue felt as a firm, concentric, often tender disc directly beneath the areola.
Must be distinguished from pseudogynaecomastia (fatty enlargement without a glandular disc) and from male breast carcinoma, which is typically hard, eccentric and painless.
Physiological forms occur in neonates, at puberty and in older men, and the majority of pubertal cases regress spontaneously within one to two years.
Results from a relative excess of oestrogen action over androgen action on breast tissue, whatever the underlying cause.
Drugs are a leading cause: examples include spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine, anti-androgens, some antipsychotics, and recreational agents such as cannabis and anabolic steroids.
Pathological causes include hypogonadism, chronic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, thyrotoxicosis and hormone-secreting testicular or adrenal tumours.
A careful history for drugs, alcohol and systemic disease with testicular examination is central to the assessment.
Management targets the cause; persistent or cosmetically distressing gynaecomastia may be treated medically in the proliferative phase or by surgical excision or liposuction.
reference.pathophysiology: Gynaecomastia arises when the balance between stimulatory oestrogen and inhibitory androgen action on breast tissue shifts in favour of oestrogen, driving proliferation of ductal epithelium and periductal stroma. This may follow increased oestrogen production or peripheral aromatisation, reduced androgen production or action, displacement of oestrogen from binding proteins, or blockade of androgen receptors by drugs. Early (florid) lesions show ductal hyperplasia with loose cellular stroma and are potentially reversible, whereas long-standing disease becomes fibrotic and hyalinised and responds poorly to medical therapy. The physiological peaks of the neonatal period, puberty and older age each reflect transient or age-related alterations in this hormonal balance.
additionalDifferentials: Neurofibroma or other benign chest-wall tumour
Metastatic deposit to the male breast
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of breasts, testes and for signs of systemic disease
Serum testosterone, oestradiol, LH and FSH
Prolactin, thyroid function and liver and renal function tests
Beta-hCG and alpha-fetoprotein if a germ-cell tumour is suspected
Testicular ultrasound where a testicular lesion is suspected
Breast ultrasound and mammography when malignancy cannot be excluded clinically
Core biopsy of any suspicious or eccentric hard mass
redFlags: Hard, eccentric or fixed mass rather than a symmetrical subareolar disc
Skin dimpling, nipple retraction, ulceration or bloody nipple discharge
Rapid unilateral enlargement in an older man
A palpable testicular mass suggesting an oestrogen-secreting tumour
reference.prognosis: Physiological and drug-induced gynaecomastia frequently resolve once the trigger is removed, especially if treated during the early proliferative phase. Long-standing fibrotic disease tends to persist and may require surgery, but the condition itself is benign.
pitfalls: Mistaking eccentric male breast carcinoma for benign gynaecomastia
Failing to examine the testes and missing a hormone-secreting tumour
Overlooking a culprit medication or recreational drug in the history
Expecting medical therapy to work on long-standing fibrotic disease
Labelling fatty pseudogynaecomastia as glandular gynaecomastia without palpating a disc

management: Identify and remove the cause, withdrawing or substituting offending drugs such as spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine, anti-androgens, cannabis or anabolic steroids
Treat underlying pathology, with testosterone replacement for confirmed hypogonadism and management of thyrotoxicosis, chronic liver disease or chronic kidney disease
Resect a hormone-secreting testicular or adrenal tumour where identified
Consider medical therapy in the early painful proliferative phase with a selective oestrogen-receptor modulator such as tamoxifen or with an aromatase inhibitor
Reassure and observe physiological cases, most of which regress spontaneously
Offer surgery such as subcutaneous mastectomy or liposuction for long-standing fibrotic, large or distressing disease
Exclude male breast carcinoma when the mass is hard, eccentric, fixed or associated with skin or nipple change, and refer to endocrinology or breast surgery as appropriate
